problem:
The following table shows some values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the interval $[2,12].$

| $x$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ | $10$ | $12$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $5$ | $3$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ |

Use the left Riemann sum, with the four subintervals indicated by the data, to approximate the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[2,12].$

First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $-3\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =-\frac{2}{3\text{i}} \\  & =-\frac{2(-3\text{i})}{(3\text{i})(-3\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{6\text{i}}{-9{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6\text{i}}{9} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

 

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\frac{2}{3}\text{i}=0+\frac{2}{3}\text{i},$ the magnitude is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=0$  and $y=\frac{2}{3}$ is positive, $z$ lies on the positive direction of the $y$-axis. So,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

   

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=\frac{2}{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))
$$
